entries.title: Jura Forest Porosity Study
entries.description: An investigation into the transitional borders and functional layering of forest edges in the Jura region.
entries.full_description: This field research examines the spatial, ecological, and legal definitions of forest boundaries across the Jura range. By mapping micro-vegetation transitions alongside timber rights, the project highlights how human maintenance subtly shapes rural landscapes. The study establishes a multi-tiered analytical methodology that bridges cartographic documentation, historical boundary tracing, and ecological field survey techniques. Rather than treating the woodland perimeter as a rigid line on an administrative zoning map, the research proposes a framework of environmental gradient—a threshold where agricultural pasture, managed silviculture, and unmanaged secondary growth overlap in a continuous state of flux. Through rigorous seasonal sampling, the project records microclimatic variations, light penetration depths, and edge-species distribution patterns across distinct geology. Particular focus is directed toward historical clearings and pasture-forest matrices (Weidewälder), where centuries of timber gathering and cattle grazing have produced highly porous ecosystem interfaces. These transitional zones exhibit distinct micro-spatial qualities: canopy density thins incrementally, understory shrub layers expand, and soil moisture gradients alter microhabitats for fauna. Beyond physical mapping, the investigation analyzes the regulatory frameworks that govern Swiss forest borders under federal forestry laws, municipal land-use plans (Bau- und Zonenordnung), and local agricultural easements. By juxtaposing statutory setback distances against actual bio-topographical features, the research exposes critical friction points between administrative spatial planning and dynamic botanical succession. The project concludes with a series of drawn spatial sections, axonometric taxonomy diagrams, and land-management recommendations. These proposals suggest flexible zoning overlays that allow controlled ecological succession within suburban and agricultural border zones, demonstrating that forest edges can serve as active spatial filters rather than static visual boundaries.

entries.title: Minimalist Timber Pavilion
entries.description: A lightweight wooden structure designed for community gathering.
entries.full_description: Constructed entirely using local larch and modular joists, this pavilion serves as a temporary shelter for outdoor workshops. The assembly requires zero metal fasteners, relying instead on traditional joinery techniques. Designed as a study in tectonic efficiency and material circularity, the structure measures six by twelve meters in plan, defined by a repetitive structural grid that allows rapid manual assembly and disassembly. Primary columns and roof beams are crafted from untreated Swiss larch, chosen for its natural resin content and high resistance to exterior weather conditions without synthetic chemical treatments. The interlocking joinery draws inspiration from traditional alpine carpentry, utilizing mortise-and-tenon connections, lap joints, and tapered hardwood pegs that tighten under structural load. To elevate the pavilion above groundwater while minimizing site impact, the structural footings consist of precast concrete piers set onto compacted gravel beds, avoiding wet concrete pours directly into soil. The roof canopy features lightweight timber battens set on a gentle six-degree pitch, covered by an translucent corrugated membrane that diffuses direct sunlight into soft, uniform interior illumination. Throughout the workshop season, the interior space functions as an open assembly floor for woodworking demonstrations, community discussions, and outdoor exhibition events. The modular framing grid allows wall panels or acoustic screens to be slotted into column grooves as seasonal needs change. At the conclusion of its operational lifecycle, every timber member can be unpegged without structural degradation, enabling full structural reuse, repurposing, or eventual clean biodegradation without leaving metallic or adhesive waste behind.

entries.title: Urban Infill Architecture
entries.description: Exploring high-density residential housing solutions within tight municipal lots.
entries.full_description: Addressing urban density challenges, this design utilizes narrow floor plates and expansive light wells to bring natural daylight deep into a five-story residential building located within a dense historic block. Constrained by firewall boundaries on three sides and a narrow seven-meter street frontage, the intervention reimagines domestic circulation and spatial hierarchy inside restricted city footprint. The structural strategy relies on a hybrid frame of exposed recycled concrete and glulam floor diaphragms, minimizing floor plate thickness while maximizing interior vertical clearance. Central to the layout is a double-height central atrium line with lime plaster and light-reflecting glass panels, functioning as both a passive ventilation chimney and a daylight funnel for core living spaces. Living areas are oriented toward the open street façade and rear garden courtyard, while service cores, stairwells, and utility infrastructure are compressed along party walls. The street elevation features vertically proportioned windows set within deep timber-clad reveals, referencing traditional urban townhouse rhythms while providing passive shading against low summer sun angles. Each apartment unit adopts a flexible open-plan layout where lightweight sliding partitions can reconfigure floor plates from a single open studio into a two-bedroom dwelling as tenant needs evolve over time. High-performance thermal envelope assemblies, triple-glazed timber-aluminum window frames, and integrated heat recovery ventilation systems ensure low operational energy consumption. By demonstrating how challenging leftover urban sites can yield high-quality, light-filled living spaces, the project offers a repeatable archetype for soft densification in historic inner-city contexts.

entries.title: Workshop Process Loop
entries.description: Visual document detailing manual craft techniques and hand tool joinery.
entries.full_description: A visual document following two weeks of prototype fabrication in the workshop, capturing the rhythmic process of hand-planing, joint cutting, and timber assembly. This photographic and diagnostic study focuses on the tactile relationships between timber craft, tool geometry, and material response during manual fabrication. Conducted within a communal woodworking studio, the project records the step-by-step transformation of rough-sawn ash and oak boards into precision structural joinery. High-speed macro photography, time-lapse sequences, and physical drawing logs capture the subtle nuances of hand woodworking: the sound frequency changes of Japanese pull saws cutting across grain, wood chip formation under hand planes set at varying bedding angles, and micro-adjustments made when fitting dry tenons into mortises. Beyond physical documentation, the document establishes an analytical comparative index mapping tool maintenance routines, blade sharpening angles, and human energy input against machine-processed timber elements. Special attention is paid to grain orientation, natural timber tension, and movement caused by ambient workshop humidity shifts. The resulting publication serves both as a pedagogical manual for traditional woodworking techniques and as a theoretical reflection on the agency of hand tools in contemporary digital architecture. By illustrating how material intuition informs design decision-making during prototype iterations, the research argues for retaining physical craft methodologies as an essential counterweight to automated parametric modeling.

entries.title: Mountain Topographic Mapping
entries.description: Custom vector contour generation and open-source map styling.
entries.full_description: Using high-resolution open topographic data, this series translates alpine terrain profiles into crisp vector art suitable for print and mobile navigation interfaces. The mapping project processes raw digital elevation models (DEMs) provided by national cartographic agencies, extracting contour lines at fine five-meter intervals across severe high-altitude relief. Through custom algorithmic filtering script pipelines developed in Python and GIS platforms, raw point-cloud noise is smoothed without sacrificing critical geomorphological detail such as ridge lines, glacial cirques, alluvial fans, and rock faces. The cartographic design language intentionally strips away extraneous urban symbols, focusing exclusively on landform contours, hydrographic networks, and vegetation density layers. Vector linework is categorized using subtle line weight hierarchies and vector hypsometric tinting: thin hair-lines define subtle slope undulations, while heavy index contours mark hundred-meter elevations. Designed for cross-platform utility, the vector dataset was adapted for large-format screen printing on technical weatherproof fabrics as well as vector tile rendering in low-power mobile mapping applications used for alpine navigation. The series includes analytical case studies covering three distinct alpine topographies—glaciated granite massifs, eroded limestone karst plateaus, and forested foothills—demonstrating how cartographic abstraction can enhance user spatial orientation and terrain comprehension in complex mountain environments.

entries.title: Exhibition Space Installation
entries.description: Spatial layout design for a gallery archive retrospective.
entries.full_description: Designing freestanding display walls and lighting grids to showcase architectural models, original drawings, and video projections within a repurposed industrial gallery space. The intervention navigates the expansive scale of a former concrete warehouse, establishing an intuitive sequence of exhibition rooms using minimal structural intervention. Standardized aluminum trusses suspend overhead track lighting and canvas baffle panels, controlling ambient light levels while defining distinct spatial zones without constructing permanent floor-to-ceiling partitions. Display walls are fabricated from lightweight oriented strand board (OSB) mounted on reusable steel stud framing, arranged in an offset pinwheel plan that guides visitors through chronological archive themes. Integrated vitrines and cantilevered timber ledges support delicate architectural models at varied sightlines, allowing visitors to examine structural joinery and material textures from multiple angles. High-definition projections cast archival footage and digital twin walkthroughs directly onto micro-textured plaster wall segments, creating a dynamic dialogue between static technical drawings and temporal media. By utilizing modular, pre-fabricated structural components, the entire installation was assembled on site in three days and can be fully reconfigured or recycled for future museum retrospectives.

entries.title: Alpine Refuge Cabin
entries.description: An off-grid emergency mountain shelter constructed at high elevation.
entries.full_description: Engineered to withstand extreme alpine weather conditions, this high-altitude shelter provides self-sufficient accommodation for mountaineers and environmental research teams. Located at an elevation of 2,800 meters, the building envelope features an aerodynamic octagonal geometry designed to deflect high-velocity winds and minimize winter snowpack accumulation around its perimeter. The structure utilizes a prefabricated cross-laminated timber (CLT) frame wrapped in an exterior skin of standing-seam zinc paneling, offering exceptional thermal mass, weather protection, and structural resilience against seismic activity and rockfall risks. The building foundation consists of steel ground screws anchored directly into granite bedrock, eliminating the need for extensive excavation or heavy concrete transport in fragile alpine ecosystems. Inside, the space is organized around a central heat-retention stone stove, surrounded by tiered sleeping berths, fold-down dining tables, and integrated gear storage compartments. Electric power is supplied by integrated photovoltaic panels mounted on the south-facing roof slope, backed by a battery storage system engineered to operate in sub-zero temperatures. Rainwater and meltwater collection systems route water through multi-stage filtration units to provide potable supply, while dry composting toilets reduce wastewater production to zero. Through compact spatial planning and high-performance building physics, the refuge demonstrates off-grid autonomy in harsh climatic contexts.

entries.title: Cooperative Housing Prototype
entries.description: A flexible residential housing model based on shared amenities and adaptable unit layouts.
entries.full_description: Developed as an urban housing model for a non-profit building cooperative, this multi-family project prioritizes communal living, long-term tenure stability, and low carbon footprint. The six-story timber-hybrid building features sixty individual residential units arranged around a central open-air atrium, which functions as the social heart of the community. To maximize spatial efficiency, individual private apartments are kept compact, ranging from one-bedroom flats to cluster housing modules, while generous communal facilities are distributed throughout the building. Shared amenities include a commercial-grade kitchen and dining hall, laundry lounges, children's playrooms, a communal workshop, and a shared rooftop garden designed for urban agriculture. Spatial flexibility is achieved through a structural column grid that eliminates load-bearing interior partition walls; non-structural walls are constructed using dry clay blocks and wood-fiber insulation, allowing units to be combined or divided as household sizes change over time. The street façade utilizes unpainted larch cladding paired with integrated planting balconies that support climbing vegetation, enhancing local biodiversity and reducing urban heat island effects. Rainwater harvested from the roof irrigates the courtyard garden and flushes building toilets, while a groundwater heat pump connected to a roof-mounted solar array supplies winter heating and summer cooling. This project provides a sustainable model for communal urban living.

entries.title: Industrial Heritage Adaptive Reuse
entries.description: Transforming a 19th-century textile factory into a vibrant cultural center.
entries.full_description: This adaptive reuse project transforms a historic 19th-century brick textile factory into a multi-disciplinary cultural hub featuring artist studios, performance spaces, and exhibition galleries. Preserving the industrial character of the original masonry shell, the design strategy inserts contemporary structural interventions made of blackened steel, glass, and raw concrete. The central factory nave, previously occupied by heavy machinery, is cleared to form a double-height public hall that connects all building wings and opens toward an adjacent river promenade. Existing cast-iron columns and timber roof trusses were fully restored on site, while damaged masonry arches were carefully repaired using salvaged brickwork. To meet contemporary energy efficiency standards without altering the historic exterior brick elevation, internal insulation layers composed of aerated lime plaster and vapor-permeable wood-fiber panels were applied directly to interior walls. Double-glazed steel-framed windows match original industrial mullion profiles, maintaining light quality while improving thermal performance. The interior layout provides adaptable workspace configurations: lightweight steel mezzanine levels inserted into high-ceiling bays double usable floor area, hosting local craft associations and creative startups. Through precise structural interventions and material juxtaposition, the project bridges industrial history and contemporary urban culture.

entries.title: Parametric Brick Façade System
entries.description: Computational design exploration of robotic bricklaying and shadow dynamics.
entries.full_description: This research project investigates the intersection of computational design algorithms and automated robotic masonry fabrication, developing a textured brick façade system that optimizes passive solar shading and ventilation. Utilizing visual programming tools, custom algorithms calculate individual brick rotation angles across a curved façade, producing a dynamic pattern of light and shadow that changes throughout the day. Each brick is precisely positioned and offset by a six-axis industrial robot arm fitted with a custom pneumatic gripper, allowing complex spatial gradients to be assembled without physical timber guide templates. The resulting screen wall acts as a porous building envelope: open mortar gaps between rotated bricks admit natural daylight and encourage cross-ventilation while blocking direct solar heat gain during peak summer afternoons. Physical prototypes were fabricated using locally sourced terracotta bricks and high-strength lime mortar, testing structural load capacity, wind pressure resistance, and thermal performance under simulated atmospheric conditions. Digital twin simulations were calibrated alongside physical thermal camera imagery, validating the algorithm's ability to lower cooling loads in warm climates. The system demonstrates how traditional masonry materials can be reinterpreted through robotic fabrication, delivering bespoke architectural envelopes with material efficiency.

entries.title: Timber Grid-Shell Roof Structure
entries.description: A double-curved timber canopy covering a public transportation hub.
entries.full_description: Spanning over forty meters across a regional bus terminal, this double-curved timber grid-shell roof offers a light, column-free canopy that protects commuters from weather while showcasing timber engineering. Constructed from thin, continuous glulam laths laid out in an intersecting diagonal grid, the shell geometry derives its structural strength from double curvature form-finding algorithms. The laths were bent into position using low-energy active bending techniques before being clamped at nodes with custom aluminum junction nodes. The entire roof assembly is supported on perimeter V-shaped steel columns that anchor into concrete foundations, transferring vertical loads and wind forces efficiently into the earth. The timber structure is clad in a high-transparency ETFE cushion system that provides light transmission while shielding the timber lattice below from moisture and UV degradation. During fabrication, advanced digital timber milling allowed for precut lath nodes and prefabricated modular sub-assemblies, reducing on-site construction time to three weeks. Embedded environmental sensors monitor structural deflection, moisture content, and temperature variations in real time, providing diagnostic data to maintenance engineers. The pavilion stands as an example of low-carbon infrastructural design, combining sustainable timber engineering with digital fabrication.

entries.title: Subterranean Archive Gallery
entries.description: Underground extension for a museum storage facility and study room.
entries.full_description: Designed as an underground extension to a historic municipal museum, this subterranean gallery and archive facility provides climate-controlled vault storage and public study rooms beneath an existing urban park. By placing the expansion underground, the project preserves the public green space above while taking advantage of natural geothermal mass to maintain stable humidity and temperature conditions required for delicate paper and textile preservation. Access to the underground facility is provided by a concrete entrance pavilion located at the edge of the park, where a grand open-stairwell leads visitors into a sequence of subterranean galleries. The interior walls feature exposed board-formed concrete finished with light-reflective mineral washes, creating a contemplative atmosphere suitable for viewing historical documents and architectural drawings. Overhead light cannons penetrate the park lawn above, directing natural sunlight down into subterranean exhibition corridors and reading rooms without exposing sensitive archival objects to direct solar radiation. Advanced HVAC systems operate with minimal energy input due to ground-coupled thermal stability, regulating interior conditions to strict archival standards. This subterranean gallery expands public cultural access while minimizing surface construction footprint.

entries.title: Modular Timber Footbridge
entries.description: A lightweight pedestrian bridge spanning a natural river valley.
entries.full_description: Spanning twenty-four meters across a mountain stream, this pedestrian bridge uses a modular timber truss configuration designed for remote assembly in protected natural reserves. Constructed from regionally harvested larch and glulam tension chords, the bridge structure was engineered as a kit of lightweight parts that could be transported to the site using small electric utility vehicles, avoiding heavy crane access or road construction through sensitive terrain. The truss geometry utilizes an inverted King-post system, where compression forces are carried by top timber members while tension is managed through stainless steel rod ties anchored into cast steel shoe joints. The bridge deck consists of modular serrated oak planks that provide slip-resistant footing for hikers and cyclists, while allowing rainwater and snowmelt to drain through deck gaps. Integrated LED strip lighting concealed within the timber handrails illuminates the walkway path at night without spilling light pollution into the surrounding forest habitat. Stainless steel mesh safety netting frames the sides, offering high transparency across the canyon scenery. The entire structure was erected on site within five days, providing an durable crossing solution.

entries.title: Urban Climate Micro-Oasis
entries.description: Landscape design mitigating high summer heat in dense paved plazas.
entries.full_description: This landscape installation addresses summer urban heat island effects in a paved city plaza through a combination of dense tree canopies, water misting networks, and permeable paving surfaces. Designed as a temporary intervention during peak summer months, the project converts three hundred square meters of asphalt into a comfortable public oasis. The spatial layout centers around modular timber seating platforms surrounded by potted shade trees, including hornbeam and birch, which provide immediate canopy coverage and evapotranspiration cooling. Embedded within the timber seating modules are high-pressure fog nozzles that release fine water vapor at regular intervals, reducing local ambient temperatures by up to five degrees Celsius without wetting surrounding surfaces. Below the timber decking, recycled gravel beds collect surface runoff during summer rainstorms, storing water for urban tree irrigation. Solar-powered environmental sensors record temperature, humidity, and public foot traffic data throughout the summer, transmitting performance analytics to city planners to inform permanent climate adaptation interventions. The project demonstrates how tactical urbanism interventions can improve public comfort in heat-vulnerable urban centers.

entries.title: Bioclimatic Residential Villa
entries.description: A single-family residence designed for passive solar gain and natural ventilation.
entries.full_description: Situated on a south-facing hillside slope, this single-family house utilizes passive solar principles, heavy thermal mass, and natural cross-ventilation to eliminate active air conditioning requirements. The building form is stepped into the natural slope, partially embedding lower living levels into the earth to take advantage of ground-coupling insulation. The north elevation is heavily insulated with minimal fenestration to minimize winter heat loss, while the south elevation features floor-to-ceiling triple-glazed windows that collect passive solar heat gain during winter months. Deep overhangs and automated exterior venetian blinds are calibrated to block high-angle summer sun, preventing interior overheating. The structural frame is constructed from raw rammed earth walls sourced from excavated site clay, paired with exposed wooden ceiling beams. The rammed earth walls serve as thermal mass, absorbing heat during the day and re-radiating it into interior spaces during cold alpine nights. Natural air ventilation is achieved through operable skylights set at the top of a central open stair tower, creating a stack effect that draws cool air from shaded lower garden patios throughout the living spaces. A green roof planted with native sedum species manages rainwater runoff while providing additional thermal insulation.

entries.title: Floating River Research Station
entries.description: A mobile pontoon platform monitoring water quality and river ecology.
entries.full_description: Designed for ecological research teams studying river health, this mobile floating laboratory moves along urban river corridors to collect water samples, record micro-plastic contamination, and monitor aquatic habitats. Built on a modular pontoon hull constructed from marine-grade aluminum, the vessel supports an enclosed laboratory space, living quarters for two researchers, and an open deck for deploying water sampling equipment. The superstructure is framed in lightweight timber clad in corrugated aluminum panels, designed for minimal draft to navigate shallow river tributaries. Onboard power is generated by a combination of roof-mounted solar photovoltaic arrays and a micro-hydro kinetic turbine deployed beneath the pontoon hull, tapping continuous river current energy when anchored. An onboard water purification system processes river water for domestic use onboard, while onboard wastewater is treated through a closed-loop biological filtration system. Laboratory spaces feature vibration-isolated workbench surfaces, digital microscopy equipment, and real-time telemetry systems that transmit water quality data directly to environmental research databases. The floating station serves as a visible public educational beacon, hosting student workshops and public demonstrations at urban river landings to raise awareness of freshwater conservation.
